newsitem.title: INDIA: Decade of political scandals in India.
newsitem.headline: Decade of political scandals in India.

text.p: The criminal cheating case in which former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao has been named is the latest in a series of scandals that have rocked Indian politics in the past decade.
Following are summaries of the major political scandals:

BOFORS SCANDAL - In 1987, then prime minister Rajiv Gandhi's government was hit by allegations that Swedish arms manufacturer AB Bofors had paid kickbacks to officials to gain a $1.3 billion artillery contract. The opposition accused Gandhi of covering up the probe into the scandal, which was seen as contributing to the defeat of Gandhi's Congress party in 1989 general elections. The allegations are still under investigation.

SECURITIES SCANDAL - India's biggest ever financial scandal erupted in April 1992. Bankers and brokers were accused of colluding illegally to siphon $1.3 billion from the inter-bank securities market to fuel a boom on the Bombay Stock Exchange. The scandal weakened Rao's government, with two cabinet members resigning after adverse remarks linked them to the scandal in a parliamentary probe.

SUGAR SCANDAL - In April 1994, Rao's government allowed the duty-free import of sugar, banned since August 1993, sparking opposition allegations that imports had been delayed to allow domestic mills to reap enormous profits. Food Minister Kalpnath Rai lost his job in the row.

TELECOMMUNICATIONS SCANDAL - Opposition parties paralysed parliament in late 1995, alleging then communications minister Sukh Ram had favoured a little-known Indian firm in opening up the state monopoly over telecommunications. The Supreme Court dismissed the allegations and paved the way for privatisation. In August, federal agents found more than $1 million in cash in two of Sukh Ram's homes. Sukh Ram, accused of causing losses to the government by favouring a firm that won an equipment bid and of having assets disproportionate to his income, was arrested earlier this month on his return from a trip to Britain. He said the money belonged to the Congress party and has denied any wrongdoing. He was put in New Delhi's Tihar jail pending trial.

HAWALA SCANDAL - An $18 million political bribery scandal in January 1996 forced seven of Rao's ministers and two governors to resign after investigators charged that a "hawala," or illegal foreign exchange dealer, paid more than 100 bureaucrats and ruling party and opposition politicians bribes in exchange for favours. The scandal was widely seen as contributing to the defeat of Congress in general elections this year.

VOTE-BUYING SCANDAL - The opposition said lawmakers of the regional Jharkand Mukti Morcha party were paid $100,000 to vote against a 1993 no-confidence motion, which Rao's Congress-led government survived by a wafer-thin margin. Earlier this year, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) filed a case accusing Rao and other Congress leaders of buying the votes. They have denied any wrongdoing.

UREA SCANDAL - The CBI in June named one of Rao's sons, P.V. Prabhakara Rao, in a $40 million kickback scandal related to the import of urea fertiliser from Turkey that never arrived. Prabhakara Rao, questioned by the CBI, denied the charges.

CHEATING SCANDAL - In July, a New Delhi criminal court judge summoned Rao to testify in a cheating case involving expatriate Indian Lakhubhai Pathak, who testified he paid $100,000 to a Rao acquaintance in 1983 in a failed try for a government contract. Rao denied any involvement. A special court upheld the summons on September 21 and ordered Rao to appear as a co-accused on September 30 on charges of criminal conspiracy to cheat. The Supreme Court excused Rao from appearing at Monday's hearing.

ST KITTS CASE - The CBI charged Rao and three others on September 26 in a forgery case involving an alleged 1989 attempt to tarnish the reputation of V.P. Singh, an opposition leader who became prime minister. The case involves the alleged falsification of bank documents to show that Singh's son, Ajeya Singh, had a secret bank account with large amounts of money on the Caribbean island of St Kitts. At the time, V.P. Singh was spearheading an anti-corruption campaign against the government. He became prime minister at the end of 1989 after Congress lost general polls. Officials later cleared Ajeya Singh of charges that he had violated foreign exchange and anti-corruption laws. Rao was not believed to have commented publicly on the case, which was due to be taken up by a New Delhi court on October 1.
